notes:
I've gathered substantial material from the allowed sites. Let me now compile the verse-by-verse notes, drawing from what each source actually says.

---

# Daniel 6 – Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## v. 1 – *"Now it pleased Darius to appoint 120 satraps to rule throughout the kingdom…"*

- **Historical context**: This picks up from Daniel 5:31, where Darius the Mede began his reign after the fall of Babylon (539 BC). The "head of gold" (Babylon) has given way to the "chest and arms of silver" (Medo-Persia), fulfilling Nebuchadnezzar's dream in Daniel 2. Judah has been in exile nearly 70 years; Daniel is now in his 80s. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_6_commentary)

- **Who is Darius?** Secular history has no clear record of a "Darius the Mede" in this period. Three main theories exist: (a) "Darius" was simply another name for **Cyrus** the Persian; (b) Darius was **Cambyses**, son of Cyrus, who governed Babylon under his father; (c) Darius was **Gubaru** (also spelled Ugbaru), a general whom Cyrus appointed as governor over Babylon immediately after its capture. "Darius" may be an honorific title meaning "holder of the scepter." Ancient documents show Gubaru had power to make appointments, assemble armies, levy taxes, and possess palaces. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-6/) (https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_6_commentary)

- **The 120 satraps**: A satrap was a Persian official who governed on behalf of the king. Critics have noted that the Greek historian Herodotus says Darius I divided the empire into only 20 satrapies. But Daniel speaks of 120 individual *satraps* (officials), not "satrapies" (provinces). This harmonises with the Nabonidus Chronicle, which states Gubaru installed sub-governors in Babylon immediately after the fall. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_6_commentary)

- **The king's motive**: The phrase "so that the king would not suffer loss" (v. 2) indicates Darius feared corruption. He wanted a system of accountability to prevent satraps enriching themselves at his expense through fraud or tax evasion. (https://bible.org/book/export/html/476)

## v. 2 – *"…and over them three administrators, including Daniel…"*

- **Daniel as "first"**: The KJV renders this "of whom Daniel was first," suggesting he held pre-eminence among the three commissioners. The arrangement created a chain of accountability: the 120 satraps reported to the three commissioners, who audited their accounts so the king would suffer no financial loss. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/6.htm)

- **Continuity from Babylon**: Ellicott notes that if there had been a triumvirate in Babylon (Daniel 5:7, 29), Darius continued the form of government he found and retained Daniel in the post to which Belshazzar had promoted him. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/daniel/6.htm)

- **God's preservation**: Precept Austin notes that Daniel had been in the banquet hall the night Babylon fell, wearing a purple robe and gold necklace marking him as the third ruler. Yet he survived. "God's man is immortal until God has fulfilled His purposes in and through that man." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_6_commentary)

## v. 3 – *"Soon, by his extraordinary spirit, Daniel distinguished himself…"*

- **"Extraordinary spirit"**: Gill notes this means a spirit of knowledge of civil affairs, prudence in managing them, and integrity throughout his conduct — not necessarily the "spirit of grace and piety" that a pagan king could not judge. The Aramaic word *yattir* means excellent, outstanding, superior. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/6.htm) (https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_6_commentary)

- **Ellicott's rendering**: "He outshone the others." The pronoun "this" before Daniel's name points him out as the favoured one. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/daniel/6.htm)

- **Planned promotion**: Darius intended to set Daniel over the *entire* kingdom — effectively making him viceroy or prime minister. This public knowledge of the planned promotion stirred the jealousy that drives the plot. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-6/)

- **Integrity defined**: Precept Austin expands on "integrity" — from the root "integer" (a whole number). A person of integrity is undivided, the same in private as in public, with congruence between "life" and "lips." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_6_commentary)

## v. 4 – *"Thus the administrators and satraps sought a charge against Daniel…"*

- **Impeccable character**: The conspirators examined Daniel's professional life thoroughly and "could find no charge or corruption." Daniel was "faithful" — no fraudulent expense accounts, no scandals, no questionable deals, no negligence. Spurgeon is quoted: "As for Lord Fair-Speech, Lord Time-Server, Mr. Smooth-Man… the entire company of them will be swept away when the Judge comes." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-6/)

- **Not sinless, but blameless**: Enduring Word clarifies this does not mean Daniel was sinless in an absolute sense; he was especially blameless in his professional conduct. The world "is a very poor critic of my Christianity, but it is a very sufficient one of my conduct" (Maclaren). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-6/)

- **Motivation beyond jealousy**: Bible.org argues that Daniel's ability threatened the other officials, but more so his *honesty*. Corrupt leaders saw that if Daniel rose above them, their opportunities to siphon funds from the king's revenue would end. "They could neither corrupt Daniel nor deceive him." (https://bible.org/book/export/html/476)

## v. 5 – *"…'We will never find any charge against this Daniel, unless we find something against him concerning the law of his God.'"*

- **The backhanded compliment**: These men knew Daniel so well they recognised the only way to trap him was through his religious devotion. Every Christian should ask whether others could say the same about them. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-6/)

- **Jealousy as root**: Ellicott identifies this conspiracy as "evidently the result of jealousy on the part of the other officers at the advancement of Daniel." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/daniel/6.htm)

- **Integrity that blocks corruption**: Precept Austin notes that besides jealousy, Daniel's incorruptibility restricted the other officials' opportunities to steal from the king. His integrity was the real threat. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_6_commentary)

- **Baptist reading (Garner-Howes)**: These men "entered collusion agreement" with feigned love for the king. "Though they cared not if he died that day, they were out for the kill." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/daniel-6.html)

## vv. 6–7 – *"So the administrators and satraps went together to the king…"*

- **A flagrant lie**: They claimed "All the royal administrators, prefects, satraps, advisers, and governors have agreed." This was false — Daniel, one of the three chief administrators, was not consulted. The lie was part of the trap. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-6/) (https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_6_commentary)

- **The religious-political trap**: Ellicott explains the object of the decree was political as well as hostile towards Daniel. By consenting, Darius would acknowledge the Babylonian system of theology whereby the king was "the living manifestation of all the gods." This flattered the king's vanity and prevented him from perceiving the plot against Daniel. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/daniel/6.htm)

- **Why 30 days?** Archer (quoted in Enduring Word) suggests the proposal seemed a statesmanlike measure to unify the former Babylonian domain under Persian authority. The time limit of one month seemed reasonable — short enough that the king would not scrutinise it carefully. Clarke adds the real object was to destroy Daniel while making the king "a god for thirty days." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-6/)

- **Baptist reading (Garner-Howes)**: "How honorable and loyal by exaggeration they made it sound! But how deceitful, scheming, lying and devious was their intent!" Compares them to the spirit of antichrist (Revelation 13:15). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/daniel-6.html)

## vv. 8–9 – *"…sign the document so that it cannot be changed—in accordance with the law of the Medes and Persians…"*

- **Irrevocable decrees**: In the Medo-Persian system, once a king formally signed a decree, even he could not change it. This was because the king was thought to speak for the gods, who could never be wrong and thus never needed to change their minds (see also Esther 8:8). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-6/)

- **"Sign the writing"**: Ellicott notes the literal sense is "record the decree" — put it in writing so there could be no possibility of recall. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/daniel/6.htm)

- **The king's fault**: Darius should have known better. The Pulpit Commentary notes that the king's vanity prevented him from seeing the trap. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/daniel/6.htm)

- **NET Bible textual note on v. 6 (Aramaic v. 7)**: The Aramaic verb *rĕgash* occurs three times in this chapter (vv. 6, 11, 15). Its meaning is widely disputed. Suggestions range from "to come thronging" to "to act in agreement for a duplicitous goal." The ancient versions vary considerably. NIV/NCV render it "went as a group"; NRSV "conspired and came to the king." (https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/dan6_notes.htm)

## v. 10 – *"Now when Daniel learned that the document had been signed, he went into his house…"*

- **Not altered by the decree**: Daniel neither increased his praying (which could be pride or courting martyrdom) nor decreased it (which would be compromise). He simply continued "as he had done before." Walvoord is quoted: "This was not the act of a person courting martyrdom but the continuation of a faithful ministry in prayer which had characterized his long life." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-6/)

- **Praying toward Jerusalem**: This followed Solomon's dedication prayer in 1 Kings 8:30, 33, 35, where Solomon asked God to hear His people's prayers when they prayed "toward this place" (the temple). Daniel kept the focus on God's covenant promises even when the temple lay in ruins. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-6/) (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/daniel/6.htm)

- **Three times daily**: Corresponds to Psalm 55:17 ("Evening, morning, and noon I cry out"). Daniel knelt — a posture of humility and begging. He gave thanks as well as making petitions. Spurgeon: "Prayer and praise should always go up to heaven arm in arm, like twin angels walking up Jacob's ladder." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-6/)

- **"As was his custom since early days"**: This phrase (in the NKJV rendering) reveals that Daniel's crisis-response was simply his lifelong habit. Morgan is quoted: "The occasional is always affected by the habitual." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-6/)

- **Why public?** Bible.org lists five reasons Daniel did not pray secretly: (1) He had no opportunity to protest the law; (2) the issue was a matter of public law, so violation must be public; (3) private disobedience would have been hypocritical; (4) his lifelong habit was known to his enemies; (5) the law implied something utterly contrary to God's law — making that point required public violation. (https://bible.org/book/export/html/476)

- **Piper (Reformed Baptist) on "open disobedience"**: "Notice how blatant Daniel's disobedience is. It is, as we say, in your face.… This was an open act of disobedience to the civil authority. It was a public act of putting God before the king's decree.… Keep in mind that there is no explicit commandment that one must pray on one's knees at an open window three times a day. This was Daniel's conviction about God's will, not an explicit command in the Bible." (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/subjection-to-god-and-subjection-to-the-state-part-3)

- **Precept Austin**: "Prayer is a good place to go when we find ourselves being tempted. Daniel's continual communion with the living God kept him prepared for unexpected testing." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_6_commentary)

## vv. 11–13 – *"Then these men went as a group and found Daniel petitioning…"*

- **Found exactly as expected**: The conspirators knew Daniel's habits and "found Daniel praying and making supplication before his God" — exactly as they anticipated. For Daniel, prayer was both communion with God (*praying*) and pleading for His will (*making supplication*). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-6/)

- **"Daniel, one of the exiles from Judah"**: The accusers deliberately demean Daniel by referring to him not as a royal administrator but as a captive — "one of the exiles from Judah." This was a racial and political slur meant to diminish his standing before the king. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-6/) (https://bible.org/book/export/html/476)

- **Baptist reading (Garner-Howes)**: The enemies acted as "peeping toms and spies against Daniel" who "assembled and caught him in the privacy of his home, praying to his God." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/daniel-6.html)

## v. 14 – *"As soon as the king heard this, he was deeply distressed…"*

- **"Greatly displeased with himself"**: Enduring Word notes the NKJV rendering and comments that Darius showed an admirable quality — instead of blaming others, he knew he was at fault. "Like Darius, our foolish decisions often haunt us. Often all we can do is pray and ask God to mercifully and miraculously intervene when we make foolish decisions." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-6/)

- **Laboured until sundown**: According to ancient eastern custom, execution was carried out on the evening of the day the accusation was made and found valid. Darius worked as long as he could to find a legal loophole. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-6/)

- **Bible.org**: Darius "was deeply distressed and set his mind on delivering Daniel; and even until sunset he kept exerting himself to rescue him." The king genuinely valued Daniel and was anguished at what his own pride had caused. (https://bible.org/book/export/html/476)

## v. 15 – *"…'Remember, O king, that by the law of the Medes and Persians no decree… can be changed.'"*

- **The trap closes**: The conspirators return to remind the king of the unchangeable nature of Medo-Persian law. They had designed the decree precisely so that even the king, once he realised Daniel was the target, could not rescue him. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-6/) (https://bible.org/book/export/html/476)

## v. 16 – *"So the king gave the order, and they brought Daniel and threw him into the den of lions. The king said to Daniel, 'May your God, whom you serve continually, deliver you!'"*

- **Darius' faith**: The king expressed a hope — born out of Daniel's testimony — that Daniel's God would deliver him. The phrase "whom you serve continually" highlights Daniel's consistent witness. "Many of us occasionally display godly character and wisdom before the world, but counteract the good by then being bad. Daniel's testimony was made by continual service." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-6/)

- **Darius' helplessness**: The king had tried his best but failed. His words amount to: "Now it is up to your God." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-6/)

- **Baptist reading (Garner-Howes)**: The king's remark is a "witness" — even a pagan king recognised Daniel's "continual" service. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/daniel-6.html)

## v. 17 – *"A stone was brought and placed over the mouth of the den, and the king sealed it with his own signet ring…"*

- **Dual purpose**: The sealing with both the king's signet and those of his nobles may have been partly to protect Daniel from enemies who might try to kill him if the lions didn't, and partly to ensure nobody could tamper with the den. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-6/)

- **Parallel to Jesus' tomb**: Many commentators note the parallel — a stone sealed over the entrance, a nobleman's signet guaranteeing no tampering, and a miraculous deliverance from what appeared to be certain death. Enduring Word points to Christ's death, resurrection, and vindication. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-6/)

## v. 18 – *"Then the king went to his palace and spent the night fasting. No entertainment was brought before him, and sleep fled from him."*

- **Daniel slept better than Darius**: Enduring Word comments that "undoubtedly, Daniel had a better night's rest than Darius." Daniel did not need to start praying on this occasion because the habit was already deeply ingrained. Spurgeon: "In any case he must have had a glorious night. What with the lions, and with angels all night to keep him company, he was spending the night-watches in grander style than Darius." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-6/)

- **NET Bible textual note on "entertainment"**: The Aramaic word *dakhavah* is "a crux interpretum" (a difficult interpretive issue). Suggestions include "music," "dancing girls," "concubines," "table," or "food" — all uncertain. The translation "entertainment" is deliberately vague and followed by many modern versions (NASB, NIV, NCV, NLT). (https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/dan6_notes.htm)

- **Fasting**: Darius's fasting may not have been a religious act but reflected his deep distress. He could not eat, enjoy entertainment, or sleep. (https://bible.org/book/export/html/476)

## vv. 19–20 – *"At the first light of dawn, the king got up and hurried to the den of lions…"*

- **"O Daniel, servant of the living God"**: Darius uses the remarkable phrase "the living God" — striking coming from a heathen king. Ellicott connects this to 1 Samuel 17:36. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/daniel/6.htm)

- **Weak faith**: Ellicott observes that Darius' faith is "very weak." In v. 16 he had a vague hope; by v. 20 that hope seems to have died out (note the tentative "has your God… been able to deliver you?"). Yet later (v. 26) his confession becomes stronger than Nebuchadnezzar's (Daniel 4:37). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/daniel/6.htm)

## vv. 21–22 – *"…'O king, may you live forever! My God sent His angel and shut the mouths of the lions.'"*

- **Respectful response**: Daniel's first words are not "I told you so" but the respectful court greeting "O king, may you live forever!" Despite the injustice, Daniel maintained respect for the king's office. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-6/)

- **The angel**: Daniel attributes his deliverance to an angel sent by God who "shut the lions' mouths." Ellicott cross-references Psalm 34:7, 10 and Daniel 3:28. Trapp (quoted in Enduring Word) speculates on *how* the angel stopped the lions — "whether by the brightness of his presence, or threatening them with his finger… or by causing in them a satiety, or by working upon their fantasy, we need not inquire." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-6/) (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/daniel/6.htm)

- **Twofold innocence**: Daniel declares he was "found innocent in His sight" (before God) and "I have done no wrong against you, O king" (before the king). Daniel broke the king's decree but did not wrong the king. This is what some call "obedient disobedience." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-6/) (https://bible.org/book/export/html/476)

- **Baptist reading (Garner-Howes)**: "Obedience to God is compatible with loyalty to kings and civil governments" — citing Matthew 22:21; 1 Peter 2:17; Acts 24:16. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/daniel-6.html)

## v. 23 – *"The king was overjoyed and gave orders to lift Daniel out of the den, and… no wounds whatsoever were found on him, because he had trusted in his God."*

- **"Because he had trusted in his God"**: The text explicitly attributes Daniel's preservation to his faith. Hebrews 11:33 lists Daniel among those "who by faith stopped the mouths of lions." Gill explains this does not refer to a particular act of faith at the moment of the miracle, but to Daniel's "general trust and confidence" in God. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/6.htm)

- **Faith and righteous cause together**: Enduring Word notes an "instructive order" — "The power of God sent an angel to protect Daniel in response to a prayer of faith coming from a consistent, abiding walk." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-6/)

- **Baptist reading (Garner-Howes)**: After medical examination, "no manner of hurt at all was found upon him. Because he trusted in his God" — citing Proverbs 3:3-5 and Hebrews 13:5. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/daniel-6.html)

## v. 24 – *"At the command of the king, the men who had falsely accused Daniel were brought and thrown into the den of lions—they and their children and wives…"*

- **Severity of Persian law**: This was brutal but consistent with ancient Persian customs. Ammianus Marcellinus (4th-century Roman historian) wrote: "The laws among them are formidable… by which, on account of the guilt of one, all the kindred perish." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-6/)

- **Proof of the miracle**: The lions "overpowered them and crushed all their bones before they reached the bottom." This proved there was no natural reason the lions spared Daniel — they were genuinely hungry and savage. The miraculous nature of Daniel's deliverance is underlined. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-6/)

- **Poetic justice**: This illustrates the cross in reverse (the guilty perish in place of the innocent) and the principle of Psalm 7:14–16 — the wicked fall into the pit they dug for the righteous. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-6/)

- **Baptist reading (Garner-Howes)**: "Vengeance belongs to the Lord and He does repay evil" — citing Deuteronomy 19:19; Proverbs 19:5; Romans 12:19. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/daniel-6.html)

- **Modern scholarship note**: Constable observes the chapter's structure is chiastic — the death of Daniel's colleagues (C') mirrors their plan for his death (C), with God's deliverance at the centre. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-6.html)

## vv. 25–27 – *"Then King Darius wrote to the people of every nation and language… 'I hereby decree that in every part of my kingdom, men are to tremble in fear before the God of Daniel…'"*

- **A pagan confession**: Like Nebuchadnezzar before him (Daniel 3:28–30; 4:34–37), Darius issues a decree praising the God of Israel. The language is remarkably Scriptural — Ellicott attributes this to Daniel's likely involvement in composing the decree. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/daniel/6.htm)

- **"The living God"**: Darius declares God is "the living God, and He endures forever; His kingdom will never be destroyed, and His dominion will never end." This echoes Daniel 4:34. The title "living God" contrasts the true God with the dead idols of Babylon and Persia. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-6/)

- **"The God of Daniel" — not yet "my God"**: Enduring Word notes a diagnostic point: "It isn't enough to say, 'the God of Daniel.' Saving faith says, 'the God of Darius.'" Darius acknowledges God's power but we cannot be certain of his personal saving faith. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-6/)

- **"Unto the end"**: Ellicott explains this means "the end of all the heathen kingdoms which shall arise upon the earth, or, in other words, the setting up of the kingdom of the Messiah." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/daniel/6.htm)

- **Pattern of the book**: Enduring Word traces a repeated pattern through Daniel: God's people stand firm, God honours them, pagan rulers proclaim God's greatness. The pattern occurs in chapters 1 (v. 20), 2 (vv. 46–47), 3 (vv. 28–30), 4 (vv. 34–37), 5 (v. 29), and now 6. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-6/)

## v. 28 – *"So Daniel prospered during the reign of Darius and the reign of Cyrus the Persian."*

- **Does this mean Darius = Cyrus?** Some take "the reign of Darius and the reign of Cyrus the Persian" to identify Darius as Cyrus himself (reading the "and" epexegetically, meaning "even"). Others maintain they were two distinct rulers whose reigns overlapped (539–530 BC for Cyrus, 539–525 BC for Darius the Mede/Gubaru). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-6/)

- **NET Bible note**: "The identity of this Darius is disputed. Some take the name to be referring to Cyrus, understanding the following vav ('and') in an epexegetical sense ('even'). Others identify Darius with a governor of Babylon known from extra-biblical records as Gubaru, or with Cambyses, son of Cyrus. Many scholars maintain that the reference is historically inaccurate." (https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/dan6_notes.htm)

- **Precept Austin**: Daniel prospered "both materially and in the Divine service of his prophecies." It was in the third year of Cyrus that Daniel received the visions of chapters 10–12. "He was prospered both materially and in the Divine service." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_6_commentary)

- **Daniel 1:21 parallel**: The book opened with "Daniel remained there until the first year of King Cyrus" (1:21). Now chapter 6 closes with Daniel prospering through the reign of Cyrus. This forms an inclusio around the historical section of Daniel (chapters 1–6). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_6_commentary)

---

## TRADITION-SPECIFIC NOTES

### Reformed / Baptist (Piper via Desiring God)
Piper draws a lesson on civil disobedience and the limits of submission to the state: Daniel's disobedience was "blatant" and "in your face" — an open act of putting God before the king's decree. Yet he also notes that Daniel's specific practice (praying on his knees at an open window three times a day facing Jerusalem) was *not* an explicit biblical command; it was "Daniel's conviction about God's will." This is relevant for discerning when civil disobedience is warranted — it's not only for explicit biblical commands but also for convictions of conscience grounded in God's will. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/subjection-to-god-and-subjection-to-the-state-part-3) (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-limits-of-submission-to-man)

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word, David Guzik)
Guzik emphasises the miraculous nature of the deliverance — the angel, the mouths being shut, the instant destruction of the accusers — as genuine supernatural intervention. He explicitly ties the arc of the chapter to Christ's death, resurrection, and vindication. The emphasis on habitual faithfulness rather than crisis heroics is a key pastoral application. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-6/)

### Baptist (Garner-Howes, StudyLight)
The Baptist commentary emphasises the sovereignty of God in vengeance, the compatibility of obedience to God with loyalty to civil government, and the importance of Daniel's "continual" service as his testimony. There is also a strong eschatological note comparing the conspirators' decree to the spirit of antichrist (Revelation 13:15). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/daniel-6.html)

### Modern Scholarship (NET Bible, Constable via StudyLight)
- **Darius identity problem**: The NET Bible notes frankly that "many scholars maintain that the reference is historically inaccurate," while also presenting the alternative identifications (Cyrus, Gubaru, Cambyses). (https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/dan6_notes.htm)
- **Chiastic structure**: Constable notes the chapter is arranged in a chiasm centred on God's deliverance. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-6.html)
- **Linguistic cruxes**: The NET Bible flags difficult Aramaic words — *rĕgash* (to come by agreement / conspire) and *dakhavah* (entertainment / music / dancing-girls) — where modern versions vary considerably. (https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/dan6_notes.htm)
- **Critical attacks**: Constable and Barnes both note Daniel 6 has been heavily targeted by rationalistic critics, primarily because of the Darius problem and the miraculous element. Barnes devotes extensive sections to defending authenticity. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-6.html) (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/daniel-6.html)
